lotl.label: What's Going On With the Leafs
lotl.body: August in Toronto is usually a hush, and this year the club is leaning into it. Patrick O'Sullivan has been named director of NHL development - a tidy, revealing hire that says the Maple Leafs are still trying to sharpen the pipeline while the roster sits in the deep offseason. There are no games on the board, no standings to chase, and no distractions from the work of filling out the bottom of the lineup and nurturing the kids. The talk around Morgan Rielly has gone quiet, which is its own kind of news in a market that lives on noise. The Leafs finished 32-36-14, so the mandate is obvious: get younger, get cleaner, get sturdier. What matters now is camp in September, where the prospects will start earning or losing their places.

lotl.label: What's Going On With the Jays
lotl.body: A club in the dead zone of August doesn't get to daydream; it has to build. Toronto's most notable move is the one that already changed the board - the Blue Jays swung a trade for José Soriano, a power arm acquired from the Angels for Arjun Nimmala, Eddie Micheletti Jr. and Angel Rivero. That is the kind of hard, expensive wager front offices make when they think the next contending window is opening, not closing. The Jays' finished season is gone, but the roster math is not: they must sort out the rotation, the middle infield and how much more pitching they can buy without hollowing out the farm. The early offseason chatter around Daulton Varsho and other pieces only sharpens the issue. What matters next is whether Toronto keeps pushing for arms - or starts protecting its prospect capital.

lotl.label: What's Going On With the Raptors
lotl.body: Quiet is the right sound for this franchise right now - but it is not idle. The Kawhi Leonard saga remains the storm cloud hanging over everything, and that unresolved business still shapes the Raptors' summer more than any scrap of chatter from the market. Toronto's record is finished, and the work now is cleaner and harder: sorting out the roster around Immanuel Quickley's volume, RJ Barrett's extension path, and whether the front office wants more shot creation or more ballast. The camp clock is already ticking, with Media Day set for September 28 and training camp in Quebec City at Université Laval's PEPS complex. Until Leonard is settled, every other move is just table setting.

lotl.label: What's Going On With the Commanders
lotl.body: Camp has already drawn a hard line up front - one injury, and the whole picture changes. Laremy Tunsil's torn triceps has flipped the Commanders' left tackle plan on its head, forcing Brandon Coleman back to tackle after his move inside and leaving Andrew Wylie in the frame if the season opened tomorrow. That is the sort of bruising pivot that exposes every weak seam in August. Washington is still sorting a roster built for competition, not comfort, with the receiver room also alive - Stefon Diggs is in the mix, and the battle for WR2 and WR3 is crowded. Nick Allegretti's calf has only thinned the interior line further. What matters now is whether Coleman stabilizes the edge before the preseason starts to sort the real depth chart.

article.title: Monday's Skate
paragraphs: The Leafs named Patrick O'Sullivan their director of NHL development, a promotion announced Sunday after three seasons as a development coach working with the NHL roster. Another Leafs note worth watching is the fading of Morgan Rielly trade talk, a sign the offseason has cooled around one of Toronto's core defenders.

The Blue Jays are still in offseason mode, but their scrappiness showed up again in a game that went to extras, and that edge should carry into the next stretch of daily play. The Raptors are also deep into their offseason, with attention on the Kawhi Leonard saga and a question that matters for Immanuel Quickley: how many triples per game he will try. For the Commanders, Brandon Coleman's 18 starts at left tackle have helped produce 11 wins, while Week 2 of camp has already sorted out a few early winners and losers.
